what: A scheduler starts jobs at set times or intervals, like every hour or every night at 2am. Cron is the classic way to write those times.
like: Like an alarm clock with a rota: it rings on time, and the rota says exactly one person gets up to do the job.
why: Runs repeating work (reports, re-crawls, cleanups, re-scoring) with no human pressing a button
Turns a big daily target into a steady, predictable flow of work
A durable scheduler remembers missed runs and catches up after downtime

nodes.t: Leader or lock|only one copy fires
AI answer engines|steady rate, no spikes

steps.d: A cron expression has five fields: minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week. 0 * * * * means at minute 0 of every hour.
Many scheduler copies run for safety, but one must fire. A leader election or a lock row, plus a recorded run id, stops the double-run problem.
3.6 million prompts a day is about 42 a second. Instead of firing all at midnight, the spreader gives each job a random offset across the window.
Each customer gets a quota per hour, so one big account cannot fill the queue and starve everyone else.
Workers pull from the queue and call the engines. Each job has a key like tenant+prompt+hour, so a run that fires twice writes one result.
The durable state knows which runs were missed. A catch-up window decides which still run, and they drain at the normal rate, not all at once.

choices.d: Plain cron on one box is simple but single. Durable schedulers (Temporal Schedules, EventBridge Scheduler, Kubernetes CronJob) survive restarts and record what ran.
What if the last run is still going? Kubernetes concurrencyPolicy: Allow (default), Forbid or Replace. Temporal: Skip (default), BufferOne, BufferAll, CancelOther, TerminateOther or AllowAll.
How late may a missed run still start? Kubernetes uses startingDeadlineSeconds; Temporal uses a catch-up window. Short for fresh data, long for runs that must happen.
Spread starts with random jitter or a flexible window instead of everyone at 00:00. Temporal adds jitter per action; EventBridge has flexible time windows.
Cap jobs per customer per hour and use a fair queue, so one large tenant cannot use all the engine capacity.

instead.why: Event-driven work: run when something happens, not on the clock
Many dependent steps in order: an Airflow-style DAG, not lone cron jobs
Results needed continuously, within seconds, rather than on a timer
Pace the calls to each engine once the jobs are queued

breaks.d: Two scheduler copies both fire the same job, or a retry repeats it.
breaks.see: Duplicate rows, double the engine calls and cost for one hour
breaks.fix: Leader election or a lock, plus an idempotency key per run

breaks.d: Every job is written as 0 0 * * *, so all of them hit the engines at once.
breaks.see: A big spike of calls and 429 rate-limit errors right at 00:00
breaks.fix: Random jitter or a flexible window, spread across the day

breaks.d: Each run takes longer than the gap between runs, so runs overlap.
breaks.see: Several copies of the same job active together
breaks.fix: Forbid or Skip overlap, or make each run smaller

breaks.d: The scheduler was down and runs were skipped with no alert.
breaks.see: Gaps in the results table; missed-action metrics rising
breaks.fix: Durable scheduler, catch-up window and an alert when a run is missed

breaks.d: After an outage, every missed run fires at once.
breaks.fix: Short catch-up window, drain backlog at a capped rate

say: 3.6 million prompts a day is about 42 a second, so I schedule them as a steady flow, not a midnight batch.
A durable scheduler fires each hour's batch, with a lock or leader so only one copy runs, and a spreader adds jitter across the hour.
Each job has an idempotency key of tenant, prompt and time slot, so a double fire or a retry writes the result once.
Per-tenant quotas keep it fair, and after downtime a catch-up window decides which missed runs still matter, drained at the normal rate.

followups.q: How do you stop two scheduler instances running the same job?
followups.a: Elect one leader (for example with a lease in etcd or a database row), or take a lock per run. Still make jobs idempotent, because locks can expire and Kubernetes warns one CronJob can sometimes create more than one Job.

followups.q: Why not schedule everything at midnight?
followups.a: Everyone picks round times, so load arrives as one spike that hits rate limits. Jitter or flexible windows spread the same work evenly, so you need far less peak capacity.

followups.q: What happens to runs missed during an outage?
followups.a: It depends on the catch-up setting. Temporal defaults to one year; Kubernetes uses startingDeadlineSeconds. For fresh visibility data, skip old runs and only run the latest.

followups.q: How would you handle tenants of very different sizes?
followups.a: Give each tenant a quota per window and use a fair queue (round-robin across tenants), so small tenants are served promptly even when a large one has a big backlog.

check.q: What does the cron expression 0 * * * * mean?
check.why: The five fields are minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week. Only minute is fixed, to 0.

check.q: A CronJob run is still going when the next one is due. Which setting skips the new one?
check.why: Forbid skips the new run. Allow, the default, lets them overlap; Replace cancels the old one.

check.q: Why give each job an idempotency key?
check.a: So a job that fires twice still writes one result
d: So the cron expression is shorter
check.why: Double fires and retries happen in distributed systems. The key makes the second run a harmless no-op.

check.q: All tenants' jobs run at 00:00 and the engines return 429 errors. Best fix?
check.a: Spread start times with jitter or a flexible window
check.why: Moving the spike just moves the problem. Spreading the same work flattens the load.
